hero.intro: An Angular library that binds a UI flow to the lifecycle of its HTTP requests. A shared requestId coordinates every element and every request in the flow (buttons, forms, panels) and re-enables them together when the whole flow settles, with no manual loading flags.

install.title: Install
install.note: Requires Angular v22 or newer. Uses standalone APIs, functional HTTP interceptors and signals.

problem.intro: A common category of front-end bugs comes from the gap between a UI flow and the HTTP requests it triggers. The user starts an action; the request is in flight; the UI is still enabled; the user clicks again, or clicks a related button, or edits the form that is about to be refreshed. Duplicate or overlapping requests reach the server. The application state diverges.

symptoms.title: Symptoms
symptoms.list:
• Duplicate POST/PUT/DELETE requests from repeated interactions.
  • Follow-up refresh calls racing the mutation they were meant to reflect.
  • Related actions (Save + Reset, Submit + Refresh) that stay clickable during the same flow.
  • Ad hoc loading booleans spread across every component that talks to the network.
  • Loading flags that stay true forever when an error path forgets to reset them.
  • Disabled-state logic drifting out of sync with the actual request lifecycle.

naive.title: The naive approach
naive.text: The typical fix is a component-level boolean toggled around each request. It works for one call and one button, but it does not compose: a follow-up refresh, a related action, or a wrapper panel each need their own flag, and the flags must be manually reset on every error path.

withLibrary.title: With ngx-request-lock
withLibrary.text: A shared requestId owns the flow. Every request in the flow carries that id in its HttpContext. A functional interceptor updates a signal-backed, reference-counted service, and every directive and every wrapper bound to the same id re-enables together only when the whole flow settles. No component-level booleans, no manual reset in error handlers.

scope.title: What this library is not
scope.list:
• It does not cancel or debounce requests.
  • It does not replace HTTP-level idempotency on the server.
  • It does not implement a global spinner or toast system.

architecture.intro: The library is composed of four small pieces that communicate through Angular's own primitives: an HttpContextToken, a functional HttpInterceptorFn, a signal-backed service, and a directive. The unit of coordination is a shared requestId: it can tag one request or an entire flow of related requests, and any number of UI elements can subscribe to that lock. No external state container, no observable orchestration in user code.

buildingBlocks.title: Building blocks
buildingBlocks.list:
• REQUEST_LOCK_ID: an HttpContextToken<string | null> that tags a request with a lock identifier. Any number of requests may share the same id and count as one flow.
  • createRequestLockContext(id): builds the HttpContext to attach to the request.
  • requestLockInterceptor: a functional interceptor that reads the id from the context and drives the service.
  • RequestLockService: a singleton service holding a reference-counted map of pending requests, exposed as a Signal<boolean> per id via isPending(id). Any UI code can consume this signal to render a custom in-flight state.
  • RequestLockDirective ([ngxRequestLock]): attaches to any element that contains or is a <button>, observes isPending(requestId), and toggles the button's disabled attribute. Multiple directive instances that share a requestId all lock and unlock together.
  • provideRequestLock(): registers provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([requestLockInterceptor])) in one call.

dataFlow.title: Data flow
dataFlow.steps:
• A user action starts the flow. Every directive instance bound to the flow's requestId sets its internal isBlocked = true and applies the disabled attribute to its resolved <button>.
  • The consumer sends one or more HTTP requests whose HttpContext carries the shared requestId via createRequestLockContext(id). A follow-up refresh, a related mutation, or a chained call may all reuse the same id.
  • For every such request, requestLockInterceptor reads REQUEST_LOCK_ID from the context, calls RequestLockService.start(id), and pipes the response through finalize(() => end(id)). The service reference-counts pending requests per id.
  • isPending(id) stays true until every request tagged with that id has settled. Only then do the directives (and any wrapper reading the same signal) unblock.
  • Two safety timeouts also unblock the directive that received the click: at 500ms if no pending state was ever observed, and at 10s unconditionally.

architecture.httpContextNote: HttpContext is local. HttpContext is Angular client-side metadata attached to a request instance. It is not serialized to headers, body, or query string, and never reaches the server.

refCount.title: Reference-counted state
refCount.text: RequestLockService increments a counter per id on start and decrements it on end. Multiple concurrent or sequential requests can share the same lock id (a mutation, its automatic refresh, a related fetch), and only the last end flips isPending(id) back to false. This is what turns a per-click lock into a whole-flow lock.
refCount.note: RequestLockService.isPending(id) returns a new computed on every call. Store the returned signal in a field if you read it repeatedly in the same component.

installation.intro: This page walks through the minimum wiring needed to get ngx-request-lock running in an Angular application: install the package, register the provider, attach a shared requestId to every HTTP request in the flow, and place the directive on each interactive element that participates in that flow.

requirements.title: Requirements
requirements.list:
• Angular v22 or newer. The library declares @angular/common and @angular/core as peer dependencies at ^22.0.0.
  • Standalone APIs, functional HTTP interceptors, and signals must be available. They are the default in v22.
  • The directive generates its requestId with crypto.randomUUID(), which requires a secure context (HTTPS or localhost) in the browser.

install.title: Install
install.text: Install the package from npm. There are no runtime dependencies other than tslib.
install.peerNote: The library ships as an Angular Package Format build. It is tree-shakable and marked sideEffects: false.

provider.title: Register the provider
provider.text: provideRequestLock() is an environment provider factory that registers the functional interceptor for you. Add it to the providers array of your ApplicationConfig.
provider.warning: Do not call provideHttpClient() separately alongside provideRequestLock(). The factory already calls provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([requestLockInterceptor])) internally. A second provideHttpClient(...) in the same providers array overrides it, and the interceptor stops running.

manualProvider.title: Manual registration
manualProvider.text: If your app already configures provideHttpClient with other interceptors, skip provideRequestLock() and register requestLockInterceptor directly.
manualProvider.note: The interceptor is a plain HttpInterceptorFn. Its order relative to other interceptors is the order you pass to withInterceptors(...).

context.title: Attach the lock id to the request
context.text: The interceptor is inert by default: it only reacts to requests whose HttpContext carries a value under REQUEST_LOCK_ID. Use createRequestLockContext(id) to build that context.
context.bullets:
• REQUEST_LOCK_ID is an HttpContextToken<string | null> with a default of null.
  • createRequestLockContext(id) returns a fresh HttpContext with the token set to id. If id is falsy the context is returned empty and the request is ignored by the interceptor.
  • Requests without this context pass through untouched. The library never modifies HTTP requests it was not asked to track.

directive.title: Add the directive to the UI
directive.text: RequestLockDirective is a standalone directive with selector [ngxRequestLock] and exportAs: 'requestLock'. Import it in the consuming component's imports array and place it on every element that participates in the flow: a single button for the simplest case, or multiple related controls that should lock together.
directive.bullets:
• Each directive instance generates a stable requestId: string once, using crypto.randomUUID(). Bind [requestId] explicitly to share the same id across multiple directive instances and coordinate a whole flow.
  • Export the instance with #lock="requestLock" and read lock.requestId() when you only need a per-element lock. For a shared-flow lock, keep the id in the component (typically as a signal(crypto.randomUUID())) and bind it into every directive and every createRequestLockContext(...) call.
  • The directive locates the button to disable via elementRef.closest('button'), falling back to the first descendant <button>. It only toggles that button's disabled attribute. Non-button hosts get no DOM mutation, but the directive's lock still contributes to the shared signal, which any wrapper can consume for a visual in-flight state.

lifecycle.title: How the UI unlocks
lifecycle.text: The unlock is driven by three moving parts working together. You never call an unblock() method yourself.
lifecycle.steps:
• On the initial click, the directive that received the event sets its internal isBlocked = true and adds the disabled attribute to its resolved button.
  • requestLockInterceptor reads the id from each request's HttpContext and calls RequestLockService.start(id). Every response stream is piped through finalize(() => service.end(id)), so success, error, and unsubscription all decrement the counter. A flow that fires POST then GET under the same id counts as two starts and two ends.
  • RequestLockService holds a signal<Record<string, number>> reference-counting pending requests per id, exposed as a boolean Signal through isPending(id).
  • Inside every directive bound to that id, and any wrapper reading isPending(id), an effect observes the signal. Only when the counter reaches zero and the signal flips back to false do those consumers release: the directives remove disabled, wrappers drop their in-flight styling.

safety.title: Safety timeouts
safety.text: Two timeouts guarantee that the interactive element cannot remain permanently disabled even if no request is ever fired or the request never settles:
safety.bullets:
• 500 ms: if no pending state has been observed by this point, the interaction did not produce a tracked request and the directive unblocks. This covers actions that do not fire HTTP at all.
  • 10 s: an unconditional ceiling. If a request is still pending after ten seconds, the element is unblocked anyway.

shared.tipConfig: All snippets assume provideRequestLock() is registered in app.config.ts. See the Installation page.

directiveUsage.intro: This page shows how RequestLockDirective locks a single interactive element bound to a single HTTP request. Each directive instance generates its own requestId, tags the request via createRequestLockContext(id), and re-enables the element automatically when the interceptor sees the request settle, on success or error. For flows that span multiple elements and multiple requests, see Flow Lock Examples.

basic.title: Basic use case
basic.text: The minimum viable wiring: one interactive element, the directive, a template reference exported as requestLock, and one HTTP request whose HttpContext carries the lock id via createRequestLockContext(id). This is the single-interaction case.
basic.bullets:
• #lock="requestLock" exposes the directive instance to the template.
  • lock.requestId() is a stable UUID generated once per directive instance.
  • The element stays disabled from the interaction until the interceptor sees the request settle.

crud.title: Save, delete, form examples
crud.text: The pattern is identical for every non-idempotent action. The only things that change are the HTTP verb and the payload; the directive, the exported reference and the context helper stay the same.

directiveUsage.formNote: The submit button in the form example combines ngxRequestLock with [disabled]="form.invalid". The directive re-applies its own disabled only while the request is pending; when it re-enables the button, form validity takes over again.

pending.title: Variant: per-button pending state
pending.text: The directive disables the button while the request is in flight, but it says nothing about the button label or its icon. A common consumer need is to swap Save for Saving... and show a spinner. The library already exposes the reactive signal you need, so no directive extension is required. Read RequestLockService.isPending(lock.requestId()) and drive the template with a computed().
pending.bullets:
• viewChild.required(RequestLockDirective) gives access to the directive instance from the component class.
  • computed(() => service.isPending(lock().requestId)()) turns the shared service signal into a plain, template-friendly boolean.
  • Use @if (isPending()) in the template to swap the label and render a spinner, with no loading field and no finalize in user code.
  • Set [attr.aria-busy] during the pending state so assistive tech announces the transition.
pending.tip: This pattern is orthogonal to the disabled behavior of the directive: the button is still blocked at the DOM level, and the pending signal only drives the visual and textual state. The two work together without conflicts.

custom.title: Custom directive: loading animation
custom.text: The library keeps the visual side deliberately empty: RequestLockDirective only toggles the native disabled attribute on the nearest button. To show a spinner or a custom animation, extend the directive in your own app and override the setBlockStatus extension point.
custom.info: This directive lives in the docs app under src/app/pages/examples/loading-request-lock.directive.ts. It is deliberately separate from the library so ngx-request-lock stays styling-agnostic.
custom.usageText: Consume it exactly like the base directive; only the selector and the exported name change.
custom.warning: The base directive is not final, but its constructor injections and the @HostListener('click') live on the parent class. Do not shadow onClick and do not re-declare the click host binding in the subclass. Override only setBlockStatus.

flowLock.intro: A requestId is not tied to a single button. Bind the same id to every element that participates in the same user flow, and to every follow-up HTTP call, and they all lock and unlock together. The reference-counted service in RequestLockService guarantees that the lock only releases when every request in the flow has settled. For the single-element case, see Directive Usage.

sharedFlow.title: Flow lock: shared requestId across a page
sharedFlow.text: Bind the same id to a primary action, a related secondary action, and any follow-up refresh, and they all lock and unlock together. Below, one shared id coordinates two buttons and an automatic POST-then-GET refresh.
sharedFlow.tip: Own the id in the component (typically a signal(crypto.randomUUID())) and bind it into every [requestId] and every createRequestLockContext(...) call. Regenerate it only when you actually want a fresh flow.
sharedFlow.bullets:
• Multiple ngxRequestLock instances bound to the same id share one reference-counted lock.
  • A follow-up HTTP call that reuses the id extends the lock: the whole flow stays disabled until the follow-up also settles.
  • An error on any request in the flow still releases the lock through the interceptor's finalize. There is no manual reset to forget.
  • Any component that needs a coarser lock (an entire form, a whole page) can bind the shared id to the wrappers it cares about.

formRefresh.title: Form: POST followed by an automatic GET refresh
formRefresh.text: A common flow: submit a form, then reload the data. Both requests share one requestId, and both the submit and the refresh button remain locked until both calls have settled. No loading boolean, no manual coordination between the two subscriptions.

inFlight.title: Variant: visual in-flight state
inFlight.text: The shared requestId is also enough to render a coarser visual in-flight state, such as a dimmed panel, an overlay, or an aria-busy region, without extending the directive or introducing a loading flag. The wrapper reads RequestLockService.isPending(flowId) and reacts, while the directives keep locking their individual buttons.
inFlight.bullets:
• The wrapper is a plain element: no ngxRequestLock needed. It only consumes the pending signal.
  • Class bindings ([class.opacity-60], [class.pointer-events-none]) render the visual state; [attr.aria-busy] announces it to assistive tech.
  • The pending signal is the same one the directives observe, so the overlay and the disabled buttons are always in sync.
  • This complements the per-button pending pattern on the Directive Usage page: the directive handles per-control blocking, the wrapper handles the whole-flow chrome.
inFlight.note: The directive itself does not style anything and does not render markup on non-button hosts. The visual variant is a consumer-side pattern that composes with the directive; it is not a separate API.

why.title: Why this matters in consumer projects
why.intro: The same three primitives, ngxRequestLock, a shared requestId, and createRequestLockContext, cover every action-triggered HTTP call in an application, from a single button to a multi-request page flow. That uniformity is the whole point:
why.bullets:
• One primitive, any granularity. The same requestId can lock one button, a group of related controls, or a whole panel. You decide by choosing where to bind it.
  • No per-component boilerplate. No loading boolean, no finalize in user code, no manual reset in error handlers.
  • Correctness on error paths. The UI is re-enabled through the interceptor's finalize, so a thrown error, a 5xx response, or a cancelled subscription all leave the UI consistent.
  • Whole-flow lock for free. The service reference-counts pending requests per id, so a mutation plus its automatic refresh plus any related fetch under the same requestId only unlock together when the entire flow settles.
  • Styling stays in the app. The library ships zero CSS; the in-flight variant and the custom directive show the exact seams where visual behavior belongs.
  • Angular-native surface. HttpContext, functional interceptors, and signals, with no external state container and no RxJS orchestration in user code.
